 Several children are in critical condition due to dengue fever, requiring dialysis and mechanical ventilation.
 (Dan Tri Newspaper) - Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City has continuously saved the lives of many children with critical dengue fever, severe complications, and requiring ECMO and continuous blood dialysis.
 Báo Dân trí • 06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 Recently, the Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City admitted a 27-month-old female child, LMH, from Thanh Hoa province, with dengue fever. She was hospitalized with a continuous high fever, vomiting, and lethargy.
 Critically ill children require dialysis and ECMO treatment. 
 According to the medical history, the child fell ill 3 days prior, experiencing a continuous high fever and vomiting approximately 3 times a day. The family self-medicated the child with unknown drugs. Subsequently, the child became lethargic and was taken to the City Children's Hospital, where they were admitted to the Infectious Diseases Department for treatment.
 The antigen test results were positive for the Dengue virus.
 However, just 12 hours after admission, the child suddenly developed respiratory failure, cyanosis, mottled skin, and a drop in blood pressure. Doctors had to resuscitate the child with intravenous fluids and vasopressors. Due to the progressive respiratory failure, the patient was intubated, placed on a ventilator, and given high doses of vasopressors.
 The child was diagnosed with fulminant myocarditis and cardiogenic shock on the third day due to Dengue hemorrhagic fever, along with liver damage, and was transferred to the Intensive Care and Toxicology Unit.
 Here, the child was lethargic, with pale lips, requiring mechanical ventilation, had cold extremities, a prolonged capillary refill time of 4-5 seconds, and a weak radial pulse. Heart rate was increased, blood pressure was decreased, and echocardiography showed a continued decrease in ejection fraction (EF).
 Given the critical condition, doctors implemented intensive resuscitation with various vasopressors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and consulted with the ECMO team.
 The child was placed on a VA ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) system, connected via the right internal jugular artery and vein. 
 A 27-month-old child is in critical condition due to dengue fever (Photo: Provided by the hospital).
 During treatment, the child continued to develop complications including multiple organ failure and severe liver and kidney damage. Doctors had to combine 8 consecutive hemodialysis sessions, blood transfusions, platelet transfusions, electrolyte and acid-base balance adjustments, and medication to support liver function.
 You may also like After nearly 5 weeks on ECMO along with intensive care, continuous hemodialysis, and organ support, the child's cardiac function gradually recovered. Ejection fraction (EF) improved to 48-52%, and blood pressure stabilized during the ECMO weaning test.
 The child was weaned off ECMO, the vascular cannula were removed, then weaned off the ventilator, switched to oxygen via cannula, and then breathed ambient air spontaneously. The heart rate returned to a normal sinus rhythm, liver and kidney function recovered, and the child urinated adequately.
 After nearly two months of treatment, the child's health has improved significantly.
 According to doctors, this is a rare case of myocarditis and cardiogenic shock in a child with dengue fever. There are currently no precise figures on the frequency of this complication, as most of the medical literature only records cases from case reports and small case series. Globally , only a few cases of myocarditis and cardiogenic shock due to dengue fever in children have been treated with VA ECMO.
 Warning signs of dengue fever worsening in children. 
 Also at the City Children's Hospital, doctors recently saved the life of a 17-day-old infant suffering from dengue shock, blood clotting disorders, and severe liver damage. 
 A 17-day-old infant is in shock due to dengue fever (Photo: Provided by the hospital).
 The patient is a boy residing in Ho Chi Minh City. Before being admitted to the hospital, the child had a moderate, intermittent high fever for two days, exhibited startled reactions during sleep, and had a red rash on his skin.
 Test results showed decreased platelet count and positive dengue antigen. The child was diagnosed with dengue fever on the second day, treated with fever reducers, and continued breastfeeding.
 By the third day, the child's condition worsened; they became lethargic, irritable, had a weak radial pulse, cold extremities, and their blood pressure dropped to 60/40 mmHg. Petechiae appeared on the hands, feet, and abdomen, along with mottled skin. Laboratory tests revealed an increase in hematocrit to 45%, decreased platelets, and elevated liver enzymes.
 Doctors diagnosed the child with dengue hemorrhagic shock and severe liver damage and immediately initiated intensive shock treatment according to protocol.
 You may also like Because the patient was so young, establishing an IV line proved difficult, and the child developed bruising at multiple injection sites. The doctors continued to administer anti-shock fluids using a high-molecular-weight solution.
 Test results revealed severe coagulation dysfunction. The child received blood transfusions, platelet concentrates, and albumin to support shock management. Additionally, the child received liver support, respiratory support with oxygen, and CPAP ventilation.
 After 72 hours of treatment, the child's hemodynamic status and liver damage improved. The patient showed no further signs of bleeding, was alert, feeding well, and urinating adequately.
 Based on the above cases, doctors advise parents not to be complacent when children contract dengue fever, especially in the early days when the disease can progress rapidly and dangerous complications can appear.
 To prevent the disease, people need to actively eliminate mosquitoes and larvae, sleep under mosquito nets, and proactively monitor children's health.
 In addition to preventive measures, a dengue fever vaccine is now available for children aged 4 and older, with a schedule of two doses administered 3 months apart. Parents can take their children to vaccination centers for advice on the appropriate indications and vaccination schedule.
 Signs that indicate a child needs immediate medical attention. 
 If a child has a high fever for more than two days and exhibits any of the following signs, they should be taken to a medical facility immediately: fussiness, restlessness, tossing and turning, or lethargy; abdominal pain; nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vomiting blood, or passing black stools; cold hands and feet, lying still and not playing, refusing to breastfeed or eat.
